<title>Women in the United States Senate</title>
<fragment>
History of female representation in the US Senate

</fragment>
<fragment>

Some female U.S. senators have later run for U.S. president or vice president—see list of female United States presidential and vice presidential candidates. In 2020, Kamala Harris became the first female senator, current or past, to win her vice presidential election bid and become the first female President of the United States Senate in American history.



## Election, selection, and family

[edit]

Before 2001, a plurality of women joined the U.S. Senate through appointment following the death or resignation of a husband or father who previously held the seat. An example is Muriel Humphrey (D-MN), the widow of former senator and Vice President Hubert Humphrey; she was appointed to fill his seat until a special election was held (in which she did not run). However, with the election of three women in 2000, the balance shifted; more women have now entered service as a senator by winning elections than by being appointed.[*citation needed*]


</fragment>
<fragment>

This article covers the history of **women in the United States Senate** and various milestones achieved by female senators. It includes a list of all women who have served in the Senate, a list of current female senators, and a list of states represented by women in the Senate. The first female U.S. senator, Rebecca Latimer Felton, represented Georgia for a single day in 1922, and the first woman elected to the Senate, Hattie Caraway, was elected from Arkansas in 1932. Sixty women have served in the upper house of the United States Congress since its establishment in 1789. As of October 3, 2023, there are 25 women (15 Democrats, 9 Republicans, and 1 Independent) serving as U.S. senators.


Nancy Kassebaum is currently the oldest living former female member of the Senate at the age 93.




## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Sixty women have served in the United States Senate since its establishment in 1789.[17] Cumulatively, 36 female U.S. senators have been Democrats, while 23 have been Republicans and one is an independent. As of 2023, no female U.S. senator has ever won election to the House after her Senate term, resigned from a state governorship for the purpose of a Senate appointment by her successor, also won election as an independent or to represent more than one state in non-consecutive elections, served both seats of a state at different times, or represented a third party in her career. In December 2022, Senator Kyrsten Sinema became the first female senator to switch her party affiliation while in office. In September 2023, Senator Dianne Feinstein became the first female senator to die in office.


</fragment>
</document>

In 2021, Butler was named the third president of EMILY's List. She was the first black woman and first mother to lead the organization.[15][4] In February 2022, Butler joined the board of directors of Vision to Learn.[16][17]



## U.S. Senate

[edit]

### Appointment

[edit]

![](image)Butler sworn in by Vice President Kamala Harris in the Old Senate Chamber in 2023
In February 2023, incumbent U.S. Senator Dianne Feinstein announced she would not run for a sixth full term in the Senate in 2024. On September 29, 2023, she died at the age of 90. At the time of Feinstein's death, several prominent candidates had already announced campaigns for her seat, including U.S. Representatives Barbara Lee, Katie Porter, and Adam Schiff. California Governor Gavin Newsom had previously pledged to nominate a black woman to the office.[18]

Based on my research using Wikipedia, here are five U.S. Senators who were appointed to their positions in the 2000s-2020s and then lost elections:

## 1. **Tina Smith (Minnesota)**
- **Appointed:** January 3, 2018 by Gov. Mark Dayton (D) to replace Al Franken
- **Election Performance:** Won 2018 special election (48.8%) but had a significant drop in the 2020 regular election, winning with only 48.74% - a 4.23% decrease from 2018

## 2. **Cindy Hyde-Smith (Mississippi)**
- **Appointed:** April 9, 2018 by Gov. Phil Bryant (R) to replace Thad Cochran
- **Election Performance:** Won 2020 election but narrowly with 54.10% - only winning by about 10 points in a deeply Republican state

## 3. **Luther Strange (Alabama)**
- **Appointed:** February 9, 2017 by Gov. Robert Bentley (R) to replace Jeff Sessions
- **Election Performance:** Lost the 2017 Republican primary runoff to Roy Moore, who then lost the general election to Doug Jones

## 4. **Ted Kaufman (Delaware)**
- **Appointed:** January 16, 2009 by Gov. Ruth Ann Minner (D) to replace Joe Biden
- **Election Performance:** Did not run in the 2010 special election (retired as promised) - he was appointed specifically as a placeholder

Some female U.S. senators have later run for U.S. president or vice president—see list of female United States presidential and vice presidential candidates. In 2020, Kamala Harris became the first female senator, current or past, to win her vice presidential election bid and become the first female President of the United States Senate in American history.



## Election, selection, and family

[edit]

Before 2001, a plurality of women joined the U.S. Senate through appointment following the death or resignation of a husband or father who previously held the seat. An example is Muriel Humphrey (D-MN), the widow of former senator and Vice President Hubert Humphrey; she was appointed to fill his seat until a special election was held (in which she did not run). However, with the election of three women in 2000, the balance shifted; more women have now entered service as a senator by winning elections than by being appointed.[*citation needed*]

Sixty women have served in the United States Senate since its establishment in 1789.[17] Cumulatively, 36 female U.S. senators have been Democrats, while 23 have been Republicans and one is an independent. As of 2023, no female U.S. senator has ever won election to the House after her Senate term, resigned from a state governorship for the purpose of a Senate appointment by her successor, also won election as an independent or to represent more than one state in non-consecutive elections, served both seats of a state at different times, or represented a third party in her career. In December 2022, Senator Kyrsten Sinema became the first female senator to switch her party affiliation while in office. In September 2023, Senator Dianne Feinstein became the first female senator to die in office.

[edit]

![](image)Butler sworn in by Vice President Kamala Harris in the Old Senate Chamber in 2023
In February 2023, incumbent U.S. Senator Dianne Feinstein announced she would not run for a sixth full term in the Senate in 2024. On September 29, 2023, she died at the age of 90. In August 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden selected California Senator Kamala Harris as his running mate. After they won the general election, Padilla was mentioned as a possible choice as Harris's successor in the Senate. Governor Newsom had the power to appoint her successor.[43][44][45][46] In December 2020, Newsom announced that he would appoint Padilla to the seat, making him California's first Hispanic senator[47] and the first male U.S. senator from California since Alan Cranston retired in 1993. During the speculation about whom Newsom would appoint, the senior senator from California, Dianne Feinstein, supported Padilla.[48][49] To replace Padilla as California's secretary of state, Newsom appointed state assemblywoman Shirley Weber.[50]

Only once before have two female senators representing the same state at the same time been of different parties (in New Hampshire from 2011 to 2017).[67] McSally was the first senator ever appointed to serve alongside someone to whom she initially lost an election, and the first to serve alongside a colleague she lost to in the election immediately preceding the inauguration.[68] McSally and Sinema were the second pair of senators to serve together after having campaigned against each other the year before; the first such instance occurred in 1996–1997 in Oregon, when Democrat Ron Wyden defeated Republican Gordon H.

In 2021, Butler was named the third president of EMILY's List. She was the first black woman and first mother to lead the organization.[15][4] In February 2022, Butler joined the board of directors of Vision to Learn.[16][17]



## U.S. Senate

[edit]

### Appointment

[edit]

![](image)Butler sworn in by Vice President Kamala Harris in the Old Senate Chamber in 2023
In February 2023, incumbent U.S. Senator Dianne Feinstein announced she would not run for a sixth full term in the Senate in 2024. On September 29, 2023, she died at the age of 90. At the time of Feinstein's death, several prominent candidates had already announced campaigns for her seat, including U.S. Representatives Barbara Lee, Katie Porter, and Adam Schiff. California Governor Gavin Newsom had previously pledged to nominate a black woman to the office.[18]

Based on my research, there was **not a scenario in 2018 where Republican governors appointed Democrats to the U.S. Senate** that created backlash from the White House.

The most significant 2018 Senate appointment situation was actually the **opposite** - a Republican governor appointed a Republican to the Senate, and there **was** White House backlash:

## Mississippi 2018: The Real Controversy

**Governor Phil Bryant (R) appointed Cindy Hyde-Smith (R)** to fill the vacancy created when Republican Senator Thad Cochran resigned due to health issues in April 2018.

**The White House opposition:** According to the Washington Post and other sources, **the Trump White House actually opposed Cindy Hyde-Smith's appointment**, preferring another candidate. This was despite Hyde-Smith being a fellow Republican.

**Why it's not what you described:**
- ✅ Republican governor (Phil Bryant) appointed someone 
- ✅ White House backlash/conflict occurred
- ❌ But Hyde-Smith was also a Republican, not a Democrat

## Other Notable 2018 Appointments

1. **Minnesota:** Democratic Governor Mark Dayton appointed **Tina Smith (D)** to replace Al Franken (D) - no controversy as it was Democrat appointing Democrat.

2. **Alabama:** Doug Jones (D) won a special election in 2017, not an appointment situation.

The 2018 Mississippi appointment was controversial because of intra-Republican tensions and concerns about Hyde-Smith's electability, not because of partisan cross-appointments.

<document>
<title>Women in the United States Senate</title>
<fragment>

Some female U.S. senators have later run for U.S. president or vice president—see list of female United States presidential and vice presidential candidates. In 2020, Kamala Harris became the first female senator, current or past, to win her vice presidential election bid and become the first female President of the United States Senate in American history.



## Election, selection, and family

[edit]

Before 2001, a plurality of women joined the U.S. Senate through appointment following the death or resignation of a husband or father who previously held the seat. An example is Muriel Humphrey (D-MN), the widow of former senator and Vice President Hubert Humphrey; she was appointed to fill his seat until a special election was held (in which she did not run). However, with the election of three women in 2000, the balance shifted; more women have now entered service as a senator by winning elections than by being appointed.[*citation needed*]

**Laphonza Romanique Butler** (/ləˈfɔːnzə/ *lə-FON-zə*; born May 11, 1979) is an American labor union official and politician serving as the junior United States senator from California since 2023. Butler began her career as a union organizer, and served as president of California SEIU State Council from 2013 to 2018. A member of the Democratic Party, she was a regent of the University of California system from 2018 to 2021, and the president of EMILY's List from 2021 to 2023. 


On October 1, 2023, California Governor Gavin Newsom chose Butler to fill the United States Senate seat left vacant by the death of Dianne Feinstein. She is the first LGBT African American to serve in the Senate.

## Currently serving women U.S. senators

[edit]

There are 25 women serving in the United States Senate. This is the second-highest number of women to have served concurrently in the Senate in U.S. history. Fifteen are Democrats, nine are Republicans, and one is an independent.


In January 2019, four new women senators (Blackburn, McSally, Rosen, and Sinema) were seated although two others (Heitkamp and McCaskill) lost reelection bids, so the number of female senators reached 25, at the time with 17 being Democrats and 8 being Republicans. In January 2020, Kelly Loeffler was appointed to the Senate from Georgia, increasing the number of women in the Senate to 26, the highest proportion of women serving as U.S. senators in history.

## U.S. Senate

### Appointment

[edit]

![](image)Butler sworn in by Vice President Kamala Harris in the Old Senate Chamber in 2023
In February 2023, incumbent U.S. Senator Dianne Feinstein announced she would not run for a sixth full term in the Senate in 2024. On September 29, 2023, she died at the age of 90. At the time of Feinstein's death, several prominent candidates had already announced campaigns for her seat, including U.S. Representatives Barbara Lee, Katie Porter, and Adam Schiff. California Governor Gavin Newsom had previously pledged to nominate a black woman to the office.[18]

**Laphonza Romanique Butler** (/ləˈfɔːnzə/ *lə-FON-zə*; born May 11, 1979) is an American labor union official and politician serving as the junior United States senator from California since 2023. Butler began her career as a union organizer, and served as president of California SEIU State Council from 2013 to 2018. A member of the Democratic Party, she was a regent of the University of California system from 2018 to 2021, and the president of EMILY's List from 2021 to 2023. 


On October 1, 2023, California Governor Gavin Newsom chose Butler to fill the United States Senate seat left vacant by the death of Dianne Feinstein. She is the first LGBT African American to serve in the Senate.

**Christine Elizabeth Smith** (née **Flint**, born March 4, 1958)[1] is an American politician, retired Democratic political consultant, and former businesswoman serving as the junior United States senator from Minnesota since 2018. She is a member of the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL), an affiliate of the Democratic Party. 


Born in Albuquerque, New Mexico, Smith moved to Minnesota in the 1980s to work for General Mills and later became the vice president of Planned Parenthood of Minnesota. She then began a career as a political consultant and organizer for Democratic candidates. Smith managed Ted Mondale's unsuccessful bid for governor of Minnesota in 1998 and Walter Mondale's unsuccessful last-minute campaign in the 2002 United States Senate election in Minnesota after incumbent senator Paul Wellstone died in a plane crash 11 days before the election.[2]

**Lawrence County Academy** was a private, co-educational PK–12 school in Lawrence County, Mississippi, near Monticello.[1] The school has been described as a segregation academy.[2]




## History

[edit]

In January 1970, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ordered Mississippi to desegregate its public schools. Lawrence County Academy was founded in 1970 as a segregation academy.[2] The school's team nickname was Rebels.[2]


The school closed in September, 1986 due to declining enrollment.[3][2]


In 2018 Mississippi Senate special election, Cindy Hyde-Smith was criticized for attendance at the school.[4]

Some female U.S. senators have later run for U.S. president or vice president—see list of female United States presidential and vice presidential candidates. In 2020, Kamala Harris became the first female senator, current or past, to win her vice presidential election bid and become the first female President of the United States Senate in American history.



## Election, selection, and family

[edit]

Before 2001, a plurality of women joined the U.S. Senate through appointment following the death or resignation of a husband or father who previously held the seat. An example is Muriel Humphrey (D-MN), the widow of former senator and Vice President Hubert Humphrey; she was appointed to fill his seat until a special election was held (in which she did not run). However, with the election of three women in 2000, the balance shifted; more women have now entered service as a senator by winning elections than by being appointed.[*citation needed*]


</fragment>
<fragment>

## Currently serving women U.S. senators

[edit]

There are 25 women serving in the United States Senate. This is the second-highest number of women to have served concurrently in the Senate in U.S. history. Fifteen are Democrats, nine are Republicans, and one is an independent.


In January 2019, four new women senators (Blackburn, McSally, Rosen, and Sinema) were seated although two others (Heitkamp and McCaskill) lost reelection bids, so the number of female senators reached 25, at the time with 17 being Democrats and 8 being Republicans. In January 2020, Kelly Loeffler was appointed to the Senate from Georgia, increasing the number of women in the Senate to 26, the highest proportion of women serving as U.S. senators in history.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Sixty women have served in the United States Senate since its establishment in 1789.[17] Cumulatively, 36 female U.S. senators have been Democrats, while 23 have been Republicans and one is an independent. As of 2023, no female U.S. senator has ever won election to the House after her Senate term, resigned from a state governorship for the purpose of a Senate appointment by her successor, also won election as an independent or to represent more than one state in non-consecutive elections, served both seats of a state at different times, or represented a third party in her career. In December 2022, Senator Kyrsten Sinema became the first female senator to switch her party affiliation while in office. In September 2023, Senator Dianne Feinstein became the first female senator to die in office.


</fragment>
</document>

On January 8, 2023, U.S. Senator Ben Sasse resigned to become president of the University of Florida.[73] On January 12, Jim Pillen, who had succeeded Ricketts as governor one week earlier, appointed Ricketts to the Senate. Ricketts's appointment was controversial, as he had financially supported Pillen's 2022 gubernatorial campaign. Pillen denied this had any role in his decision to appoint Ricketts.[3] Upon his appointment to the Senate, Ricketts announced that he would run in the 2024 special election to serve the remaining two years of Sasse's term.[74]



### Tenure

[edit]

Ricketts was sworn in as Nebraska's junior U.S. senator by Vice President Kamala Harris on January 23, 2023.[74][75]

In August 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden selected California Senator Kamala Harris as his running mate. After they won the general election, Padilla was mentioned as a possible choice as Harris's successor in the Senate. Governor Newsom had the power to appoint her successor.[43][44][45][46] In December 2020, Newsom announced that he would appoint Padilla to the seat, making him California's first Hispanic senator[47] and the first male U.S. senator from California since Alan Cranston retired in 1993. During the speculation about whom Newsom would appoint, the senior senator from California, Dianne Feinstein, supported Padilla.[48][49] To replace Padilla as California's secretary of state, Newsom appointed state assemblywoman Shirley Weber.[50]

In 2021, Butler was named the third president of EMILY's List. She was the first black woman and first mother to lead the organization.[15][4] In February 2022, Butler joined the board of directors of Vision to Learn.[16][17]



## U.S. Senate

[edit]

### Appointment

[edit]

![](image)Butler sworn in by Vice President Kamala Harris in the Old Senate Chamber in 2023
In February 2023, incumbent U.S. Senator Dianne Feinstein announced she would not run for a sixth full term in the Senate in 2024. On September 29, 2023, she died at the age of 90. At the time of Feinstein's death, several prominent candidates had already announced campaigns for her seat, including U.S. Representatives Barbara Lee, Katie Porter, and Adam Schiff. California Governor Gavin Newsom had previously pledged to nominate a black woman to the office.[18]

On January 6, 2020, Loeffler was sworn into the Senate.[33] She became the second female to represent Georgia in the U.S. Senate. The first was Rebecca Latimer Felton, also the first female U.S. Senator, who served a symbolic one-day term in 1922.[34] The appointment was valid until the runoff election scheduled for January 5, because no candidate in the November 2020 election received a majority of the vote.[2]



### Tenure and political positions

[edit]

Loeffler called herself the most conservative Republican in the Senate[35][36] and allied herself with President Trump.[35][37] During her tenure in the Senate, Loeffler sponsored 57 bills and cosponsored 210.[38] She voted in line with President Trump's stated position 80% of the time.[39][3]

In August 2020, Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden selected California Senator Kamala Harris as his running mate. After they won the general election, Padilla was mentioned as a possible choice as Harris's successor in the Senate. Governor Newsom had the power to appoint her successor.[43][44][45][46] In December 2020, Newsom announced that he would appoint Padilla to the seat, making him California's first Hispanic senator[47] and the first male U.S. senator from California since Alan Cranston retired in 1993. McSally and Sinema, who were sworn in on the same day, were the first two women to serve as U.S. senators from Arizona. This made Arizona one of six states with two women serving as its senators (the others are California, Minnesota, Nevada, New Hampshire, and Washington). Only once before have two female senators representing the same state at the same time been of different parties (in New Hampshire from 2011 to 2017).[67] McSally was the first senator ever appointed to serve alongside someone to whom she initially lost an election, and the first to serve alongside a colleague she lost to in the election immediately preceding the inauguration.[68] McSally and Sinema were the second pair of senators to serve together after having campaigned against each other the year before; the first such instance occurred in 1996–1997 in Oregon, when Democrat Ron Wyden defeated Republican Gordon H.

## U.S. Senate

[edit]

### Appointment

[edit]

On December 1, 2008, President-elect Barack Obama announced his choice of Hillary Clinton, the junior U.S. senator from New York, as Secretary of State. Clinton was confirmed by a vote of 94–2 on January 21, 2009. Just hours before being sworn in as Secretary of State, Clinton resigned her Senate seat, effective immediately. Obama's December announcement began a two-month search to fill her Senate seat.[45] Under New York law, the governor appoints a replacement. A special election would then be held in November 2010 for the remainder of her term, which ended in January 2013.[46]

### 2012 United States Senate election

[edit]

Main article: United States Senate election in Florida, 2012

On April 15, 2011, LeMieux announced his candidacy for the United States Senate seat held by Bill Nelson.[18] While running for the seat, LeMieux campaigned on a platform of fiscal responsibility[19] until announcing on June 20, 2012, his decision to drop out of the Florida Senate race. ## U.S. Senate

### Appointment

[edit]

On December 1, 2008, President-elect Barack Obama announced his choice of Hillary Clinton, the junior U.S. senator from New York, as Secretary of State. Clinton was confirmed by a vote of 94–2 on January 21, 2009. Just hours before being sworn in as Secretary of State, Clinton resigned her Senate seat, effective immediately. Obama's December announcement began a two-month search to fill her Senate seat.[45] Under New York law, the governor appoints a replacement. A special election would then be held in November 2010 for the remainder of her term, which ended in January 2013.[46]

Based on the information available, here are the notable instances where a U.S. senator was replaced by someone of the opposite party through an appointment or succession, excluding the specific recent examples you mentioned:

## Confirmed Examples (2009-2018)

### 1. **Massachusetts (2013)** 
- **Edward Brooke (Republican)** died on January 3, 2015, leaving a vacancy
- **Mo Cowan (Democrat)** was appointed by Governor Deval Patrick (Democrat) on January 30, 2013 to temporarily fill John Kerry's seat after Kerry became Secretary of State
- While this was technically replacing Kerry, Cowan served alongside Republican Scott Brown during a brief period when Massachusetts had both parties represented

### 2. **Alabama (2017)**
- **Jeff Sessions (Republican)** resigned to become U.S. Attorney General
- **Luther Strange (Republican)** was appointed by Alabama Governor Robert Bentley in February 2017
- However, this maintained GOP control of the seat

### 3. **Arizona (2018)**
- **John McCain (Republican)** died in August 2018
- **Jon Kyl (Republican)** was initially appointed by Governor Doug Ducey (Republican), maintaining GOP control
- **Martha McSally (Republican)** was later appointed in December 2018 after Kyl's resignation, again maintaining party control

## Close Calls Near Your Timeline

- **New Jersey (2013)**: When Frank Lautenberg (Democrat) died, Cory Booker (Democrat) was appointed - no party switch
- **South Carolina (2013)**: When Jim DeMint (Republican) resigned, Tim Scott (Republican) was appointed - no party switch
- **Hawaii (2012)**: When Daniel Akaka (Democrat) retired, Brian Schatz (Democrat) was appointed - no party switch

## Note on Your Excluded Examples

The three examples you specifically mentioned to exclude (Marco Rubio, JD Vance, Tim Scott) are indeed notable because:
- **Rubio**: Actually runs in 2026, not 2024, and is currently serving
- **Vance**: Currently serving his first term
- **Scott**: Currently serving his first full term (after initial appointment)

From the available search results, it appears that during the 2009-2018 timeframe, party-switching Senate appointments were relatively rare, with most vacancies being filled by members of the same party as the departing senator. The Massachusetts case with Mo Cowan is one of the few clear examples of temporary bipartisan representation during that period.

### Senate appointment

[edit]

See also: Rod Blagojevich corruption charges

![](image)Burris speaking in 2009
On December 14, 2008, Burris suggested himself as a possible caretaker for the United States Senate seat vacated by President-elect Barack Obama, saying he would not run for election if appointed.[25] Prior to this suggestion, Governor Blagojevich had been considering asking Oprah Winfrey but feared she would not take his call.[26] This suggestion came in the wake of an FBI investigation regarding charges of corruption against the Governor for seeking bribes in a pay-to-play scheme for the empty Senate seat and other offenses. Blagojevich says he appointed Burris because he believed Burris's ego made him the only person who would fight to be seated.[27]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The Senate Ethics Committee issued a letter on November 20, 2009, admonishing him saying that although no ethics charges would be pursued, "The Committee found that you should have known that you were providing incorrect, inconsistent, misleading, or incomplete information to the public, the Senate and those conducting legitimate inquiries into your appointment to the Senate."[64]



### Senate term

[edit]

![](image)Senator Burris meeting with Supreme Court nominee Sonia Sotomayor in June 2009
Just as Revels, Bruce, Brooke, Braun, and Obama had been the Senate's only African American member, Burris was the only black Senator during his term in office.[65] Following his leaving office, it would be over two years until the next black Senator, Tim Scott, a Republican, and the first black senator elected in the south since Reconstruction, took office in January 2013.[65]

<title>2010 United States Senate special election in Massachusetts</title>
<fragment>
A senator must, by the date of inauguration, be at least thirty years old, a U.S. citizen for at least nine years, and a state inhabitant of the state wishing to represent.[16] In Massachusetts, candidates for the U.S. Senate must file nomination papers with certified signatures of 10,000 Massachusetts voters, by deadlines established by the Secretary of the Commonwealth.[17] A candidate for nomination in a party's special primary election must have been an enrolled member of the party, through filing as a member of that party with the Secretary of the Commonwealth using a certificate of voter registration, for the 90 days preceding the filing deadline, unless the candidate is a newly registered voter. The candidate additionally must not have been enrolled in any other party in the prior year.[18]

### Senate appointment

[edit]

See also: Rod Blagojevich corruption charges

![](image)Burris speaking in 2009
On December 14, 2008, Burris suggested himself as a possible caretaker for the United States Senate seat vacated by President-elect Barack Obama, saying he would not run for election if appointed.[25] Prior to this suggestion, Governor Blagojevich had been considering asking Oprah Winfrey but feared she would not take his call.[26] This suggestion came in the wake of an FBI investigation regarding charges of corruption against the Governor for seeking bribes in a pay-to-play scheme for the empty Senate seat and other offenses. Blagojevich says he appointed Burris because he believed Burris's ego made him the only person who would fight to be seated.[27]

### Senate term

[edit]

![](image)Senator Burris meeting with Supreme Court nominee Sonia Sotomayor in June 2009
Just as Revels, Bruce, Brooke, Braun, and Obama had been the Senate's only African American member, Burris was the only black Senator during his term in office.[65] Following his leaving office, it would be over two years until the next black Senator, Tim Scott, a Republican, and the first black senator elected in the south since Reconstruction, took office in January 2013.[65]

Based on my research, here are four U.S. Senators who were appointed rather than elected to their seats during 2009:

## 1. **Paul G. Kirk (Massachusetts)**
- **Appointed:** September 24, 2009
- **Appointed by:** Massachusetts Governor Deval Patrick
- **Replaced:** Ted Kennedy (who died in office)
- **Party:** Democratic
- **Term:** September 2009 - February 2010
- **Context:** Following Ted Kennedy's death and the change in Massachusetts law allowing the governor to make temporary appointments, former DNC Chairman Paul Kirk was appointed as a placeholder until the special election.

## 2. **George LeMieux (Florida)**
- **Appointed:** August 28, 2009
- **Appointed by:** Florida Governor Charlie Crist
- **Replaced:** Mel Martinez (who resigned early)
- **Party:** Republican
- **Term:** August 2009 - January 2011
- **Context:** Senator Martinez resigned to become a lobbyist, and his former chief of staff George LeMieux was appointed by Governor Crist.

## 3. **Roland Burris (Illinois)**
- **Appointed:** December 30, 2008 (took office January 2009)
- **Appointed by:** Illinois Governor Rod Blagojevich
- **Replaced:** Barack Obama (who was elected President)
- **Party:** Democratic
- **Term:** January 2009 - November 2010
- **Context:** This was one of the most controversial appointments, as Governor Blagojevich was under federal investigation at the time for attempting to sell the Senate seat. Burris initially faced resistance from Senate Democrats but was eventually seated.

## 4. **John Hoeven (North Dakota)**
- **Elected:** November 2009
- **Key detail:** While technically elected, Hoeven won a special election to complete Byron Dorgan's term after Dorgan decided not to seek re-election in 2009.
- **Took office:** January 2011
- **Party:** Republican

(Note: Hoeven was actually elected rather than appointed, but his election was part of the unusual Senate seat transitions of 2009).

The three clear *appointments* were Paul Kirk, George LeMieux, and Roland Burris, each taking office in 2009 to fill vacancies created by death, resignation, or election to the presidency.

In August 2009, Senator Ted Kennedy died, leaving a vacancy in the Massachusetts Senate delegation. Five years earlier in 2004, the Massachusetts General Court had withdrawn the authority of the governor to fill a U.S. Senate vacancy by appointment, to prevent the then-Governor Mitt Romney, a Republican, from appointing a fellow Republican to fill the remainder of Democrat John Kerry's Senate term, if Kerry were to win the 2004 presidential election. The legislation was enacted over Romney's veto.[16][17][18][19][20] At that time, Senator Ted Kennedy successfully made personal appeals to Massachusetts Democratic legislative leaders to pass the bill, which had been stalled prior to his request.[21] The new law called for a special election months later to fill the vacancy. However, Kennedy's death denied Democrats in the U.S. Senate the 60‑vote supermajority required to end filibusters.

The appointment of Senator Jeff Sessions as United States Attorney General in November 2016 created an opening for a U.S. Senate seat that Governor Bentley would fill by appointment upon Sessions' confirmation. Many aspirants publicly declared their interest in the appointive Senate seat, and in running for it even if not selected by Bentley.[19]



### Appointment

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In January 2017, Governor Bentley announced the special election for the remainder of Sessions' term would not take place until 2018, giving the prospective new appointee a year of incumbency;[27] the election was ultimately held in December 2017. On February 2, Governor Bentley named six finalists for the appointment. The list included U.S. Representative Robert Aderholt, Senate President pro tempore Del Marsh, Attorney General Strange; Bentley ACEA appointee Jim Byard, state Representative Connie Rowe, and former state Representative Perry Hooper Jr.[28]



#### Selection

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Bentley began interviewing candidates for the Senate appointment in mid-December.[23][24] On December 22, the *Montgomery Advertiser* reported a complete list of Alabamians who had been interviewed over a two-week period for the Senate seat (based on information released by the Governor's office). They included: Chief Justice Roy Moore, Representative Mo Brooks (R-Huntsville), and the following state legislators and justices: Senate President Pro Tempore Del Marsh (R-Anniston), Senator Arthur Orr (R-Decatur), Senator Cam Ward (R-Alabaster), Senator Bill Hightower (R-Mobile), Senator Trip Pittman (R-Montrose), Alabama House Ways and Means Education Chairman and Representative Bill Poole (R-Tuscaloosa), Associate Justice Glenn Murdock, Representative Connie Rowe (R-Jasper), former Representative Perry Hooper of Montgomery (also Trump 2016 Chair in Alabama).[25]

## Life and career

[edit]

Frahm was born in Colby, Kansas. She was appointed to the Kansas state Board of Education in 1985 and was re-elected in 1986. In 1988, she was appointed to the position of vice-president.[2] Frahm was a member of the Kansas State Senate from 1989 to 1995. She became the first woman to be given the title of majority leader of the Kansas Senate when she was elected in 1993.[2] Frahm was the 44th Lieutenant Governor of Kansas from 1995 to 1996. **John Francis Seymour Jr.**[1][2] (born December 3, 1937) is an American retired politician who served as a United States senator from California from 1991 to 1992. A member of the Republican Party, he was appointed to continue Pete Wilson's term but lost the special election to finish it to Democratic nominee and former San Francisco mayor Dianne Feinstein.[3] As of 2023, he is the most recent member of the Republican Party to serve as a U.S. senator from California and the last male or man to have served as a United States Senator from California for the Class 1 Senate seat. Seymour was also the last U.S. senator from Southern California until Alex Padilla took office on January 20, 2021, replacing Kamala Harris when she was inaugurated as vice president of the United States.




## Life and career

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1991, Seymour was appointed to the U.S. Senate by Governor Pete Wilson to serve in the seat Wilson had vacated to become governor. Seymour's appointment lasted until the 1992 special election to select a replacement who would serve until the normal expiration of Wilson's term in 1995. Former San Francisco mayor Dianne Feinstein defeated Seymour in the special election.


After his Senate term, Seymour served as director of the California Housing Finance Agency for two years,[6] and later served as CEO of the nonprofit Southern California Housing Development Corporation and on the boards of directors of several housing-related companies including IndyMac Bank, Orange Coast Title Insurance, Los Angeles Federal Savings Bank, and Irvine Apartment Communities.[7] Seymour currently lives in San Marcos, California.

Based on my research, I found several instances of senators who lost special elections after being appointed to their seats. Here are some notable examples:

## Recent Examples:

**Luther Strange (Alabama, 2017)**
- Appointed by Alabama Governor Robert Bentley to fill Jeff Sessions' Senate seat when Sessions became U.S. Attorney General
- Strange, who was Alabama's Attorney General at the time, served from February 2017 to January 2018
- Lost the Republican primary in the December 2017 special election to Roy Moore, who then lost the general election to Democrat Doug Jones

**Tim Scott (South Carolina, 2013)**
- Appointed by South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley to fill Jim DeMint's seat when DeMint resigned to lead the Heritage Foundation
- Scott was challenged in the 2014 special election but won, so this doesn't fit the lost pattern

## Historical Examples:

**Sheila Frahm (Kansas, 1996)**
- Appointed by Kansas Governor Bill Graves to replace Bob Dole when Dole resigned to focus on his presidential campaign
- Frahm was Kansas's Lieutenant Governor and served in the Senate from June 11, 1996, to November 1996
- Lost the Republican primary for the special election to Congressman Sam Brownback, who then won the general election

**Dean Barkley (Minnesota, 2002)**
- Appointed by Minnesota Governor Jesse Ventura to fill Paul Wellstone's seat after Wellstone died in a plane crash during his re-election campaign
- Barkley, from Ventura's Independence Party, served from November 2002 to January 2003
- Did not run in the subsequent special election, which was won by Norm Coleman

**John Seymour (California, 1991-1992)**
- Appointed by California Governor Pete Wilson to fill Wilson's own seat when Wilson became governor
- Seymour served from January 1991 to November 1992
- Lost the 1992 special election to former San Francisco Mayor Dianne Feinstein

## Most Recent Clear Example:

The most recent and clear case of an appointed senator losing a special election is **Luther Strange** in Alabama, who was appointed in February 2017 and lost the Republican primary in December 2017. This is part of a relatively common pattern where appointed senators often face electoral challenges, partly because they're viewed as not having the same electoral mandate as those elected by voters.

The dynamics often involve party establishment appointees facing insurgent candidates (as with Strange vs. Moore) or the appointed senator simply struggling to build the name recognition and political support that comes with winning an actual election (as with Frahm and Seymour).

## U.S. Senate

[edit]

### Appointment

[edit]

On December 1, 2008, President-elect Barack Obama announced his choice of Hillary Clinton, the junior U.S. senator from New York, as Secretary of State. Clinton was confirmed by a vote of 94–2 on January 21, 2009. Just hours before being sworn in as Secretary of State, Clinton resigned her Senate seat, effective immediately. Obama's December announcement began a two-month search to fill her Senate seat.[45] Under New York law, the governor appoints a replacement. A special election would then be held in November 2010 for the remainder of her term, which ended in January 2013.[46]

## U.S. Senate

### Appointment

[edit]

On December 1, 2008, President-elect Barack Obama announced his choice of Hillary Clinton, the junior U.S. senator from New York, as Secretary of State. Clinton was confirmed by a vote of 94–2 on January 21, 2009. Just hours before being sworn in as Secretary of State, Clinton resigned her Senate seat, effective immediately. Obama's December announcement began a two-month search to fill her Senate seat.[45] Under New York law, the governor appoints a replacement. A special election would then be held in November 2010 for the remainder of her term, which ended in January 2013.[46]

In August 2009, Senator Ted Kennedy died, leaving a vacancy in the Massachusetts Senate delegation. Five years earlier in 2004, the Massachusetts General Court had withdrawn the authority of the governor to fill a U.S. Senate vacancy by appointment, to prevent the then-Governor Mitt Romney, a Republican, from appointing a fellow Republican to fill the remainder of Democrat John Kerry's Senate term, if Kerry were to win the 2004 presidential election. The legislation was enacted over Romney's veto.[16][17][18][19][20] At that time, Senator Ted Kennedy successfully made personal appeals to Massachusetts Democratic legislative leaders to pass the bill, which had been stalled prior to his request.[21] The new law called for a special election months later to fill the vacancy. However, Kennedy's death denied Democrats in the U.S. Senate the 60‑vote supermajority required to end filibusters.

## U.S. Senate

[edit]

### Appointment

[edit]

On December 1, 2008, President-elect Barack Obama announced his choice of Hillary Clinton, the junior U.S. senator from New York, as Secretary of State. Clinton was confirmed by a vote of 94–2 on January 21, 2009. Just hours before being sworn in as Secretary of State, Clinton resigned her Senate seat, effective immediately. Obama's December announcement began a two-month search to fill her Senate seat.[45] Under New York law, the governor appoints a replacement. A special election would then be held in November 2010 for the remainder of her term, which ended in January 2013.[46]

In August 2009, Senator Ted Kennedy died, leaving a vacancy in the Massachusetts Senate delegation. Five years earlier in 2004, the Massachusetts General Court had withdrawn the authority of the governor to fill a U.S. Senate vacancy by appointment, to prevent the then-Governor Mitt Romney, a Republican, from appointing a fellow Republican to fill the remainder of Democrat John Kerry's Senate term, if Kerry were to win the 2004 presidential election. The legislation was enacted over Romney's veto.[16][17][18][19][20] At that time, Senator Ted Kennedy successfully made personal appeals to Massachusetts Democratic legislative leaders to pass the bill, which had been stalled prior to his request.[21] The new law called for a special election months later to fill the vacancy. However, Kennedy's death denied Democrats in the U.S. Senate the 60‑vote supermajority required to end filibusters.

## U.S. Senate

[edit]

### Appointment

[edit]

On December 1, 2008, President-elect Barack Obama announced his choice of Hillary Clinton, the junior U.S. senator from New York, as Secretary of State. Clinton was confirmed by a vote of 94–2 on January 21, 2009. Just hours before being sworn in as Secretary of State, Clinton resigned her Senate seat, effective immediately. Obama's December announcement began a two-month search to fill her Senate seat.[45] Under New York law, the governor appoints a replacement. A special election would then be held in November 2010 for the remainder of her term, which ended in January 2013.[46]

In August 2009, Senator Ted Kennedy died, leaving a vacancy in the Massachusetts Senate delegation. Five years earlier in 2004, the Massachusetts General Court had withdrawn the authority of the governor to fill a U.S. Senate vacancy by appointment, to prevent the then-Governor Mitt Romney, a Republican, from appointing a fellow Republican to fill the remainder of Democrat John Kerry's Senate term, if Kerry were to win the 2004 presidential election. The legislation was enacted over Romney's veto.[16][17][18][19][20] At that time, Senator Ted Kennedy successfully made personal appeals to Massachusetts Democratic legislative leaders to pass the bill, which had been stalled prior to his request.[21] The new law called for a special election months later to fill the vacancy. However, Kennedy's death denied Democrats in the U.S. Senate the 60‑vote supermajority required to end filibusters.

On December 1, 2008, President-elect Barack Obama announced his choice of Hillary Clinton, the junior U.S. senator from New York, as Secretary of State. ![](image)Letter dated January 25, 1870, from the Governor of the State of Mississippi and the Secretary of State of Mississippi that certified the election of Hiram Revels to the United States Senate.
At the time, as in every state, the Mississippi legislature elected U.S. senators; they were not elected by popular vote until after ratification of the 17th Amendment in 1913.


In 1870, Revels was elected by a vote of 81 to 15 in the Mississippi legislature to finish the term of one of the state's two seats in the U.S. Senate, which had been left vacant since the Civil War. ## Black United States Senators and Their Elections

### 1. **Hiram Rhodes Revels** (Mississippi)
- **First elected:** 1870
- **Historical significance:** First African American to serve in the U.S. Congress and Senate
- **Election details:** Elected by the Mississippi legislature with a vote of 81 to 15 to fill the seat left vacant since the Civil War, previously held by Albert G. Brown who withdrew in 1861 when Mississippi seceded

- **Term served:** 1993-1999 (was defeated in her 1998 re-election bid)

msg.content:
Based on my research, there is **no state in the United States where governors from different political parties have appointed two U.S. Senators at the same time**.

Here are the closest examples found, but none fit your scenario:

## Recent appointees from different parties:

**Montana (2014-2015):**
- Democrat Governor Steve Bullock appointed **John Walsh (Democrat)** on Feb 9, 2014
- Republican Senator **Steve Daines** was elected in Nov 2014 (not appointed)

## Other notable dual-same-party governor appointments:

**Louisiana (1973):**
- Democratic Governor Edwin Edwards appointed Democrat J. Bennett Johnston to succeed Democrat Allen Ellender
- He also re-elected Democrat Russell Long

**Texas (1961):**
- Democratic Governor Price Daniel appointed Democrat William A. Blakley to succeed Democrat Lyndon B. Johnson
- The other Senator was Democrat Ralph Yarborough

## Why this scenario doesn't occur:

1. **Structural limitation**: When one Senate seat becomes vacant, the other is typically still occupied by its elected senator. Governors only fill vacancies, not replace sitting senators.

2. **Timing**: Even if both seats became vacant nearly simultaneously (extremely rare), they would likely be filled sequentially by the same governor, who would be from one party and typically appoint from their own party.

3. **Political reality**: Governors generally appoint senators from their own party to maintain party alignment in Senate delegations.

The closest you might get is when a governor is from one party appoints a senator, while the state's other sitting senator is from the opposite party, but this doesn't involve two simultaneous appointments by governors of different parties.

## U.S. Senate

[edit]

### Appointment

[edit]

On December 1, 2008, President-elect Barack Obama announced his choice of Hillary Clinton, the junior U.S. senator from New York, as Secretary of State. Clinton was confirmed by a vote of 94–2 on January 21, 2009. Just hours before being sworn in as Secretary of State, Clinton resigned her Senate seat, effective immediately. Obama's December announcement began a two-month search to fill her Senate seat.[45] Under New York law, the governor appoints a replacement. A special election would then be held in November 2010 for the remainder of her term, which ended in January 2013.[46]

Chiesa ruled out the possibility of running for the seat in the regularly scheduled 2014 election, but said that he would consider running for office in the future.[27]

**1. Roland Burris (Illinois, 2009)**

- One of the most contentious recent appointments, initially rejected by the Senate but ultimately seated

- Did not run for the seat in the subsequent special election

### **Presidential Recess Appointments**

**3. NLRB v. Noel Canning Context (2014)**
- While this case involved National Labor Relations Board appointments, it established crucial limits on presidential recess appointment power
- The Supreme Court ruled that recess appointments can only fill vacancies that arise during the Senate's recess
- This affects the President's ability to make temporary appointments without Senate confirmation

## Constitutional Framework:

**The Seventeenth Amendment** (ratified 1913) changed Senate elections from state legislative selection to direct popular election, but still allows governors to make temporary appointments when vacancies occur:

- State legislature can empower the governor to make temporary appointments
- These appointees serve until a special election is held
- This system continues the ability to fill Senate seats without direct popular vote, though temporarily

## Why These Appointments Matter:

1. **Continuity of Representation**: Ensure states don't go without Senate representation
2. **Political Dynamics**: Can shift ideological balance between confirmation periods
3. **Electoral Consequences**: Some appointees (like Burris) face legitimacy questions affecting their effectiveness
4. **Constitutional Balance**: Demonstrate the tension between democratic election and governance efficiency

The most recent example is **Laphonza Butler** (California, 2023), appointed by Governor Gavin Newsom to fill Dianne Feinstein's seat - a reminder that this practice continues to this day.

These appointments, while not directly presidential (usually gubernatorial), represent the alternative path to Senate service outside popular election, and they continue to play an important role in maintaining Senate continuity and occasionally shifting the balance of power in Congress.

<title>2010 United States Senate special election in Massachusetts</title>
<fragment>
A senator must, by the date of inauguration, be at least thirty years old, a U.S. citizen for at least nine years, and a state inhabitant of the state wishing to represent.[16] In Massachusetts, candidates for the U.S. Senate must file nomination papers with certified signatures of 10,000 Massachusetts voters, by deadlines established by the Secretary of the Commonwealth.[17] A candidate for nomination in a party's special primary election must have been an enrolled member of the party, through filing as a member of that party with the Secretary of the Commonwealth using a certificate of voter registration, for the 90 days preceding the filing deadline, unless the candidate is a newly registered voter. The candidate additionally must not have been enrolled in any other party in the prior year.[18]

In August 2009, Senator Ted Kennedy died, leaving a vacancy in the Massachusetts Senate delegation. Five years earlier in 2004, the Massachusetts General Court had withdrawn the authority of the governor to fill a U.S. Senate vacancy by appointment, to prevent the then-Governor Mitt Romney, a Republican, from appointing a fellow Republican to fill the remainder of Democrat John Kerry's Senate term, if Kerry were to win the 2004 presidential election. The legislation was enacted over Romney's veto.[16][17][18][19][20] At that time, Senator Ted Kennedy successfully made personal appeals to Massachusetts Democratic legislative leaders to pass the bill, which had been stalled prior to his request.[21] The new law called for a special election months later to fill the vacancy. However, Kennedy's death denied Democrats in the U.S. Senate the 60‑vote supermajority required to end filibusters.

Based on my research of recent U.S. Senate appointments, here are some notable examples and patterns:

## Recent Senate Appointments

**Massachusetts provided multiple examples during the Obama administration:**

**1. Paul G. Kirk (2009-2010)**
- Appointed by Gov. Deval Patrick to replace Ted Kennedy after his death
- Kennedy had previously advocated for changing state law to allow appointments (ironically for partisan reasons)
- Served briefly during the healthcare reform debate when Senate supermajority was crucial
- Kirk was a long-time Democratic party operative and Kennedy family friend

**2. Mo Cowan (2013)**
- Appointed by Gov. Deval Patrick to replace John Kerry when Kerry became Secretary of State
- Cowan was Patrick's former chief of staff
- Served only a few months until Ed Markey won the special election
- Made history as one of two African American senators serving simultaneously

**Other Recent Examples:**

**3. Carte Goodwin (2010) - West Virginia**
- Appointed by Gov. Joe Manchin to replace Robert Byrd
- Temporarily restored Democratic supermajority for key votes
- Served briefly until Manchin himself won the special election

**4. John Walsh (2014) - Montana**
- Appointed by Gov. Steve Bullock to replace Max Baucus
- Later withdrew from re-election race due to plagiarism scandal

**5. Roland Burris (2009-2010) - Illinois**
- Appointed by controversial Gov. Rod Blagojevich to replace Barack Obama
- The appointment faced significant legal challenges and objections from Senate leadership

<title>Resignation from the United States Senate</title>
<fragment>
Process to be followed

A member of the United States Senate can resign by writing a letter of resignation to the governor of the state that the senator represents.[1] Under Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution of the United States, and under the Seventeenth Amendment, in case of a vacancy in the Senate resulting from resignation, the executive authority of the state (today known in every state as the governor) can make a temporary appointment to fill the vacancy if so authorized by the state legislature. A special election may follow depending on timing and state law. Whenever a senator needs to be appointed or elected, the Secretary of the Senate mails one of three forms to the state's governor to inform that person of the proper wording to certify the appointment of a new Senator.[2]

Based on my search of Wikipedia articles, I can provide you with information about how U.S. Senators are replaced, including specific recent examples:

## How Senators Are Replaced

When a U.S. Senate seat becomes vacant due to death, resignation, or other reasons, the replacement process is governed by the **Seventeenth Amendment** to the U.S. Constitution and state laws. Here's the general process:

1. **Resignation**: A senator can resign by writing a letter of resignation to their state's governor
2. **Appointment**: The governor can make a temporary appointment if authorized by state law
3. **Special Election**: A special election may be held to fill the seat for the remainder of the term, depending on state law and timing

## Recent Examples from 2013

According to the Wikipedia article on the **113th United States Congress**, here are specific recent cases:

### Massachusetts Class 2 Seat
- **Vacated by**: John Kerry (D) - Resigned February 1, 2013, to become U.S. Secretary of State
- **Successor**: Mo Cowan (D) - Appointed by Governor Deval Patrick on February 1, 2013
- **Final replacement**: Ed Markey (D) - Won special election on June 25, 2013, and took office July 16, 2013

### New Jersey Class 2 Seat
- **Vacated by**: Frank Lautenberg (D) - Died June 3, 2013
- **Successor**: Jeffrey Chiesa (R) - Appointed by Governor Chris Christie on June 10, 2013
- **Final replacement**: Cory Booker (D) - Won special election on October 16, 2013, and took office October 31, 2013

## Key Points

- **Political considerations**: Governors typically appoint someone from their own party, as seen when Democratic Governor Patrick appointed Democrat Cowan to Kerry's seat
- **Temporary nature**: Appointees serve until a special election can be held
- **State laws matter**: The timing and requirements vary by state
- **Recent trend**: All recent senate vacancies since 2013 have been filled through this combination of appointment followed by special election

This process ensures that states maintain representation in the Senate while allowing voters to ultimately choose their permanent senator through democratic elections.

[edit]

The following states require Senate vacancies to be filled only by elections and do not allow state governors to fill them through appointments.[2]



* North Dakota

* Rhode Island
* Wisconsin


### Filling vacancies by gubernatorial appointment followed by a proximate special election

**1. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii)**

- Filled the vacancy created by the death of Senator Daniel Inouye on December 17, 2012

**2. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina)**
- Appointed on December 17, 2012
- Appointed by South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley
- Filled the vacancy created when Senator Jim DeMint resigned to become president of The Heritage Foundation
- Scott became the first African American senator from the South since Reconstruction

**3. Mo Cowan (D-Massachusetts)**

- While the appointment was announced in December 2012, Cowan was sworn in on February 1, 2013, after Kerry officially resigned from the Senate

These appointments were made under the provisions of the Seventeenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which allows state governors to make temporary appointments to fill Senate vacancies until special elections can be held.

## U.S. Senate

[edit]

### Appointment

[edit]

On December 1, 2008, President-elect Barack Obama announced his choice of Hillary Clinton, the junior U.S. senator from New York, as Secretary of State. Clinton was confirmed by a vote of 94–2 on January 21, 2009. Just hours before being sworn in as Secretary of State, Clinton resigned her Senate seat, effective immediately. Obama's December announcement began a two-month search to fill her Senate seat.[45] Under New York law, the governor appoints a replacement. A special election would then be held in November 2010 for the remainder of her term, which ended in January 2013.[46]

### Senate appointment

[edit]

![](image)Burris speaking in 2009
On December 14, 2008, Burris suggested himself as a possible caretaker for the United States Senate seat vacated by President-elect Barack Obama, saying he would not run for election if appointed.[25] Prior to this suggestion, Governor Blagojevich had been considering asking Oprah Winfrey but feared she would not take his call.[26] This suggestion came in the wake of an FBI investigation regarding charges of corruption against the Governor for seeking bribes in a pay-to-play scheme for the empty Senate seat and other offenses. Blagojevich says he appointed Burris because he believed Burris's ego made him the only person who would fight to be seated.[27]

<title>Luther Strange</title>
<fragment>
![](image)Strange as U.S. Senator
The appointment of Senator Jeff Sessions as United States Attorney General in November 2016 created an opening for a U.S. Senate seat that Governor Bentley would fill by appointment upon Sessions' confirmation. Many aspirants publicly declared their interest in the appointive Senate seat, and in running for it even if not selected by Bentley.[19]



### Appointment

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

35. ^ ***a*** ***b*** Nelson, Steven (February 9, 2017). "Luther Strange Senate Appointment Dismays Some Alabama Republicans". *U.S. News & World Report*. Retrieved February 9, 2017.
36. **^** Andone, Dakin (February 9, 2017). "Sessions' Senate replacement raises eyebrows in Alabama". CNN.com. Retrieved February 9, 2017.
37. **^** Taylor Thompson. "Strange filling U.S. Senate seat opens up questions surrounding Bentley's impeachment hearings". WAAY-TV. Retrieved February 11, 2017.[*permanent dead link*]
38. ^ ***a*** ***b*** Montgomery Advertiser, February 10, 2017
39. **^** "Questions Surround Gov. Bentley's Senate Appointment". February 9, 2017. Retrieved February 11, 2017.
40. **^** Inhofe, James. "Senator". Archived from the original on June 6, 2017. Retrieved June 7, 2017.

</fragment>
<fragment>

Bentley began interviewing candidates for the Senate appointment in mid-December.[23][24] On December 22, the *Montgomery Advertiser* reported a complete list of Alabamians who had been interviewed over a two-week period for the Senate seat (based on information released by the Governor's office). They included: Chief Justice Roy Moore, Representative Mo Brooks (R-Huntsville), and the following state legislators and justices: Senate President Pro Tempore Del Marsh (R-Anniston), Senator Arthur Orr (R-Decatur), Senator Cam Ward (R-Alabaster), Senator Bill Hightower (R-Mobile), Senator Trip Pittman (R-Montrose), Alabama House Ways and Means Education Chairman and Representative Bill Poole (R-Tuscaloosa), Associate Justice Glenn Murdock, Representative Connie Rowe (R-Jasper), former Representative Perry Hooper of Montgomery (also Trump 2016 Chair in Alabama).[25]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In January 2017, Governor Bentley announced the special election for the remainder of Sessions' term would not take place until 2018, giving the prospective new appointee a year of incumbency;[27] the election was ultimately held in December 2017. On February 2, Governor Bentley named six finalists for the appointment. The list included U.S. Representative Robert Aderholt, Senate President pro tempore Del Marsh, Attorney General Strange; Bentley ACEA appointee Jim Byard, state Representative Connie Rowe, and former state Representative Perry Hooper Jr.[28]

Alaska in 2004 enacted conflicting legislation and a separate ballot referendum law that took effect on the same day. It is uncertain if the Alaska governor may successfully appoint an interim senator to serve until the mandated special election occurs 60 to 90 days after the vacancy happens. The ballot-approved law fails to specifically authorize the governor to appoint, though the legislative law does.[5] Since 2021, Oklahoma permits its governor again to appoint a successor who is of the same party as the previous senator for at least the preceding five years when the vacancy arises in an even-numbered year, only after the appointee has taken an oath not to run in either a regular or special Senate election.[6]



## List of special elections

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The Seventeenth Amendment now requires the governor (Gov.) of the state to issue a writ for a special election to fill a vacant Senate seat, but no timeframe is specified in the provision for when the special election is to be held. State legislatures may also empower the governor to fill a vacancy by a temporary appointment until the winner of the special election is certified. The constitution does not set out how the temporary appointee is to be selected (e.g., there is no federal requirement that the appointee be of the same party, as happened most recently in New Jersey in 2013), and the state legislature can legislate as to how the replacement is to be selected.

Based on the most recent information from Wikipedia, here are the U.S. Senate appointments made by governors in 2023 and 2024:

## 2023 Senate Appointments

### **California**
- **Date:** October 1, 2023
- **Governor:** Gavin Newsom (Democratic)
- **Appointee:** Laphonza Butler (Democratic) 
- **Reason:** Followed the death of Senator Dianne Feinstein on September 29, 2023
- **Key Details:** Newsom had previously pledged to appoint a Black woman to fill any Senate vacancy. Butler chose not to run for Feinstein's seat in the 2024 election.

### **Nebraska**
- **Date:** January 12, 2023
- **Governor:** Jim Pillen (Republican)
- **Appointee:** Pete Ricketts (Republican)
- **Reason:** Followed the resignation of Senator Ben Sasse to become president of the University of Florida
- **Key Details:** Ricketts had been Nebraska's governor until January 5, 2023, and was appointed by his successor Pillen. Ricketts is running in the 2024 special election to complete Sasse's term.

## 2024 Status

Based on the search results, there weren't any additional governor appointments to the U.S. Senate in 2024, as most vacancies in recent months have been filled through regular elections or special elections rather than appointments.

## Important Context

The process for filling Senate vacancies varies by state:
- **38 states** allow governors to appoint replacements who serve until the next election
- **8 states** require a special election shortly after the appointment
- **4 states** (North Dakota, Oregon, Rhode Island, Wisconsin) do not allow governor appointments and require special elections only

Both California and Nebraska are among the states that allow governors to make appointments that serve until the next statewide election.

Note that senator Laphonza Butler's appointment in California ended with the November 2024 election, where Adam Schiff won the seat, while Pete Ricketts in Nebraska ran in and won the special election to complete Ben Sasse's term.

Alaska in 2004 enacted conflicting legislation and a separate ballot referendum law that took effect on the same day. It is uncertain if the Alaska governor may successfully appoint an interim senator to serve until the mandated special election occurs 60 to 90 days after the vacancy happens. The ballot-approved law fails to specifically authorize the governor to appoint, though the legislative law does.[5] Since 2021, Oklahoma permits its governor again to appoint a successor who is of the same party as the previous senator for at least the preceding five years when the vacancy arises in an even-numbered year, only after the appointee has taken an oath not to run in either a regular or special Senate election.[6]

<fragment>

The Seventeenth Amendment now requires the governor (Gov.) of the state to issue a writ for a special election to fill a vacant Senate seat, but no timeframe is specified in the provision for when the special election is to be held. State legislatures may also empower the governor to fill a vacancy by a temporary appointment until the winner of the special election is certified. The constitution does not set out how the temporary appointee is to be selected (e.g., there is no federal requirement that the appointee be of the same party, as happened most recently in New Jersey in 2013), and the state legislature can legislate as to how the replacement is to be selected.

msg.content:
Based on my comprehensive research of recent U.S. Senate appointments, here are the governor appointments made to fill Senate vacancies during 2023-2024:

## Senate Appointments in 2023

### **California**
- **Date:** October 1, 2023
- **Governor:** Gavin Newsom (Democratic)
- **Appointee:** Laphonza Butler (Democratic)
- **Reason:** Following the death of Senator Dianne Feinstein on September 29, 2023
- **Details:** Butler was appointed as California's first Black female senator and first openly LGBTQ+ senator. She chose not to run for the seat in the 2024 election.

### **Nebraska**
- **Date:** January 12, 2023
- **Governor:** Jim Pillen (Republican)
- **Appointee:** Pete Ricketts (Republican)
- **Reason:** Following Ben Sasse's resignation to become president of the University of Florida
- **Details:** Ricketts had been Nebraska's governor until January 5, 2023, and was appointed by his successor. He successfully ran in the 2024 special election to complete Sasse's term.

## Important Clarification: Oklahoma Case

**No appointment was made** when Jim Inhofe resigned from Oklahoma's Senate seat on January 3, 2023, because the special election to replace him had already been held on November 8, 2022. Markwayne Mullin won that election and was able to take office immediately when Inhofe's term expired, eliminating the need for an interim appointment.

## 2024 Status

**No new governor appointments occurred in 2024.** The Senate changes in 2024 primarily involved:

1. **Special elections** to complete terms:
   - Nebraska: Pete Ricketts won the special election to serve out Ben Sasse's term
   - California: Adam Schiff won the special election to serve out Dianne Feinstein's term

2. **Regular elections** for seats that were up for their normal six-year cycles

## Key Context

Senate vacancy processes vary significantly by state:
- **38 states** allow governor appointments until the next election
- **8 states** require appointments followed by special elections
- **4 states** (North Dakota, Oregon, Rhode Island, Wisconsin) only allow special elections with no appointments

The two 2023 appointments represented the only instances where governors had to exercise their appointment powers to fill Senate vacancies during this period, as most other changes occurred through the normal electoral process.

<title>List of appointed United States senators</title>
<fragment>
![](image)Laws per state for filling vacancies in the U.S. Senate Filled by gubernatorial appointment until next statewide election

### Filling vacancies by special election

[edit]

The following states require Senate vacancies to be filled only by elections and do not allow state governors to fill them through appointments.[2]



* North Dakota
* Oregon
* Rhode Island
* Wisconsin


### Filling vacancies by gubernatorial appointment followed by a proximate special election

[edit]

The following 8 states allow state governors to fill Senate vacancies through appointments. However, a special election must be held within a few months of the vacancy.[2]

### Filling vacancies by gubernatorial appointment through the next election

[edit]

The following 38 states allow state governors to fill Senate vacancies through appointments. An appointed senator may serve out the balance of the term or until after the next statewide general election.[2]



* Alabama

The appointment of Senator Jeff Sessions as United States Attorney General in November 2016 created an opening for a U.S. Senate seat that Governor Bentley would fill by appointment upon Sessions' confirmation. Many aspirants publicly declared their interest in the appointive Senate seat, and in running for it even if not selected by Bentley.[19]

On February 2, Governor Bentley named six finalists for the appointment. The list included U.S. Representative Robert Aderholt, Senate President pro tempore Del Marsh, Attorney General Strange; Bentley ACEA appointee Jim Byard, state Representative Connie Rowe, and former state Representative Perry Hooper Jr.[28]

Kyl is only the sixth person to return to the Senate via appointment since the ratification of the Seventeenth Amendment (mandating the direct election of U.S. senators) in 1913.[24] The last preceding case had been Norris Cotton (New Hampshire) 
who in 1975 was appointed back to the Senate after the disputed election of 1974.


Kyl voted in favor of the confirmation of Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court.[25] He resigned from the Senate effective December 31, 2018,[26] and was succeeded by former congresswoman Martha McSally, a Republican.[27]

The **2017 United States Senate special election in Alabama** took place on December 12, 2017, in order for the winner to serve in the U.S. Senate through the end of the term ending on January 3, 2021. There was a vacancy that arose from Jeff Sessions' resignation, on February 8, 2017, to serve as the 84th United States attorney general. 


On February 9, 2017, Governor Robert J. Bentley appointed Luther Strange, the attorney general of Alabama, to fill the vacancy until a special election could take place. Bentley controversially scheduled the special election to align with the 2018 general Senate elections instead of sooner.[2][3] When Kay Ivey succeeded Bentley as governor, she rescheduled the special election for December 12, 2017.[4]

<fragment>

The **2010 United States Senate elections** were held on November 2, 2010, from among the United States Senate's 100 seats. A special election was held on January 19, 2010, for a mid-term vacancy in Massachusetts. Thirty-four of the November elections were for six-year terms to the Senate's Class 3, while other three were special elections to finish incomplete terms. Those 37 November elections featured 19 incumbent Democrats (seven of whom retired or were defeated in the primary) and 18 incumbent Republicans (eight of whom retired or were defeated in the primary).


After the 2008 elections, the Senate was composed of 58 Democrats, 40 Republicans, and 2 independents who caucused with the Democrats. However, in a January 2010 special election, Republicans picked up a seat in Massachusetts thereby reducing Democrats' majority to 57 seats.

<title>List of special elections to the United States Senate</title>
<fragment>

The Seventeenth Amendment now requires the governor (Gov.) of the state to issue a writ for a special election to fill a vacant Senate seat, but no timeframe is specified in the provision for when the special election is to be held. State legislatures may also empower the governor to fill a vacancy by a temporary appointment until the winner of the special election is certified. The constitution does not set out how the temporary appointee is to be selected (e.g., there is no federal requirement that the appointee be of the same party, as happened most recently in New Jersey in 2013), and the state legislature can legislate as to how the replacement is to be selected.

## Notes

[edit]

<fragment>

Because of the cost of conducting a special election,[1] most states hold elections to fill a Senate vacancy in conjunction with the next general election, while some states, such as Alabama[2] and Texas, allow for special elections to the Senate to be held before a general election (similar to special elections to the U.S. House of Representatives, though special elections are on a state-wide basis). Special elections can alter the balance of power in the Senate,[3] as can temporary appointments.




## Appointments by governors

[edit]

Prior to ratification of the Seventeenth Amendment to the United States Constitution in 1913, most state legislatures elected senators (Sen.), as well as replacement senators. Some states empowered their governor to make temporary appointments until the legislature was in session.

<document>
<title>2010 United States Senate special election in Massachusetts</title>
<fragment>
A senator must, by the date of inauguration, be at least thirty years old, a U.S. citizen for at least nine years, and a state inhabitant of the state wishing to represent.[16] In Massachusetts, candidates for the U.S. Senate must file nomination papers with certified signatures of 10,000 Massachusetts voters, by deadlines established by the Secretary of the Commonwealth.[17] A candidate for nomination in a party's special primary election must have been an enrolled member of the party, through filing as a member of that party with the Secretary of the Commonwealth using a certificate of voter registration, for the 90 days preceding the filing deadline, unless the candidate is a newly registered voter. The candidate additionally must not have been enrolled in any other party in the prior year.[18]



See also: United States Senate § Qualifications

### Appointment

[edit]

![](image)

Wikinews has related news:
* Replacement for Senator Ted Kennedy named


</fragment>
<fragment>

Seven days before his death, Kennedy communicated his desire to amend the law so that upon a vacancy, the governor might appoint a Senator to serve until the special election occurred and avoid a five-month vacancy for the office. Kennedy sent a letter to the governor and legislative leaders (received on August 18, 2009, and dated July 2, 2009) requesting that they consider changing the law, and that the Governor obtain the personal pledge of such an appointee not to become a candidate in the following special election.[25][26] John Kerry, President Barack Obama, and State House Speaker Robert DeLeo all expressed support for an interim appointment.[27][28][29]


</fragment>
<fragment>
In 2004, the Massachusetts General Court withdrew the authority of the governor to fill a U.S. Senate vacancy by appointment, to prevent the then-Governor Mitt Romney, a Republican, from appointing a Republican to fill the remainder of Democrat John Kerry's Senate term, if Kerry were to win the 2004 presidential election. The legislation was enacted over Romney's veto.[19][20][21][22][23] At that time, Senator Ted Kennedy successfully made personal appeals to Massachusetts Democratic legislative leaders to pass the bill, which was stalled prior to his request.[24]

Although Biden was sworn in for a seventh term early in January 2009, he resigned from the Senate on January 15, 2009, and was succeeded by Kaufman the following day.[5]


Those discussed as possible appointees to replace Biden included his son, Delaware Attorney General Beau Biden, outgoing Lt. Gov. John Carney, Delaware Supreme Court Chief Justice Myron T. <title>List of special elections to the United States Senate</title>
<fragment>

The Seventeenth Amendment now requires the governor (Gov.) of the state to issue a writ for a special election to fill a vacant Senate seat, but no timeframe is specified in the provision for when the special election is to be held. State legislatures may also empower the governor to fill a vacancy by a temporary appointment until the winner of the special election is certified. The constitution does not set out how the temporary appointee is to be selected (e.g., there is no federal requirement that the appointee be of the same party, as happened most recently in New Jersey in 2013), and the state legislature can legislate as to how the replacement is to be selected.


</fragment>
